items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the agriculture and markets law, in relation to the posting of security by a person from whom an animal is seized and impounded
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5727

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the agriculture and markets law, in
relation to the posting of security by a person from whom an animal is
seized and impounded

PURPOSE:

This bill seeks to improve the process for animal sheltering
organizations to responsibly meet the costs associated with caring for
the victims of animal cruelty during a criminal investigation.

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

This measure would amend AML Section 373 to authorize an impounding
organization, holding live animals as evidence on behalf of any
political subdivision of government during a criminal investigation,
to petition the court of jurisdiction for the posting of security upon
the issuance of an appearance ticket under certain circumstances, or
within a reasonable time thereafter.

The proposal would also provide much-needed clarification for certain
jurisdictions that that the petition shall be filed in the criminal
court that will hear the pending cruelty case, and assure alleged
abusers prompter access to the judicial forum, ensuring retention of
their animals while criminal charges are resolved.

JUSTIFICATION:

Most often, not-for-profit humane societies, societies for the
prevention of cruelty to animals and other sheltering organizations
care for the victims of animal abuse when they are seized from their
alleged abusers. The security posting process in current law plays an
essential role in helping to cover the significant costs associated
with caring for such victims by authorizing courts to require the
accused to place funds in an account that can be accessed by the
sheltering organization to assist with providing this essential
service.

This law, enacted decades ago, acknowledges that once cruelty or
animal fighting charges are filed, it can be several months or even
longer before the criminal case is resolved - either by a plea bargain
or by criminal trial. Indeed, the organizations that take on the care
of these animals for local governments often face daunting financial
hardship in caring for these victims, and the fiscal burden is
particularly acute when a case involves seizure of large numbers of
animals (in a dog fighting case, for example). Unlike other types of
evidence, these are living, sentient beings that require food, water,
veterinary care and other services. However, deficiencies in the
current law can inhibit the ability to truly fulfill its spirit by
impeding the manner in which sheltering organizations can meet this
duty.

Under existing law, the impounding organization in such cases - or a
district attorney acting on its behalf - may petition the court of
jurisdiction to require the accused to post security in an amount
sufficient meet all reasonable expenses expected to be incurred for


caring and providing for seized animals pending disposition of the
cruelty charges. Unfortunately, the law only allows such petition to
be filed "upon arraignment or within a reasonable time thereafter,"
which is not a problem if the person charged is taken into custody,
whereby they are arraigned within a short timeframe (typically 24
hours). However, many times when animals are seized in such cases, an
appearance ticket is issued instead, leaving the arraignment period
open-ended and at the discretion of law enforcement and the court.

Depending upon the specifics of the case and the jurisdiction,
arraignment may not occur for several days, several weeks, or in many
cases much longer. In New York City, for example, the typical wait for
an arraignment to occur is at least 6 to 8 weeks after the issuance of
an appearance ticket. This creates a clear and serious delay in the
ability to petition the court for security, thereby placing the
financial burden of caring for such animals squarely on the backs of
the impounding organization until arraignment occurs.

With that in mind, this measure would authorize the security posting
petition to be filed upon the issuance of an appearance ticket or
within a reasonable time thereafter. It would not affect or confuse
the current petition process where an alleged abuser is brought into
physical custody. The proposal would also provide much-needed
clarification for certain jurisdictions (New York City in particular)
that that the petition shall be filed in the criminal court that will
hear the pending cruelty case.

These amendments will in fact benefit not just the impounding
organization and the seized animals but also the defendant, who will
be assured prompter access to the judicial forum to ensure retention
of his animals while criminal charges are resolved. Taken together,
these measures would greatly improve the process for animal shelters
and the local governments they serve to responsibly meet the costs
associated with caring for the victims of animal cruelty.

Unable to shoulder these costs alone, many shelters are forced to
limit the assistance they can offer, which in turn creates an obstacle
to effective enforcement of cruelty and anti-fighting laws - serious
misdemeanor and felony-level crimes in New York State. If there is no
place for the seized animals to go, law enforcement often has little
choice but to weigh against seizing them in the first place - an
outcome that must be avoided wherever possible.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

90 days after enactment.

A.actClause: AN ACT to amend the agriculture and markets law, in relation to the posting of security by a person against whom certain criminal charges are pending
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5727A

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the agriculture and markets law, in relation to the
posting of security by a person against whom certain criminal charges
are pending

 PURPOSE :

This bill seeks to improve the process for animal sheltering
organizations to responsibly meet the costs associated with caring for
the victims of animal cruelty during a criminal investigation.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section one amends section 373 of the agriculture and markets law to
authorize an impounding organization, holding live animals as evidence
on behalf of any political subdivision of government during a criminal
investigation, to petition the court of jurisdiction for the posting
of security upon the issuance of an appearance ticket under certain
circumstances, or within a reasonable time thereafter.  This section
also provides that service can be completed personally or through
certified mail when a petition is filed after the issuance of an
appearance ticket, but prior to arraignment on charges. If a petition
is filed after the issuance of an appearance ticket, but prior to
arraignment on charges, if the defendant does not have counsel at the
time of arraignment, the court may appoint counsel for purposes of the
petition if such defendant is otherwise eligible for appointed counsel
for the underlying criminal offense.

Section two provides the effective date.

 JUSTIFICATION :

Not-for-profit humane societies, societies for the prevention of
cruelty to animals and other sheltering organizations are often left
to care for the victims of animal abuse when such animals are seized
from their alleged abusers. The security posting process in current
law plays an essential role in helping to cover the significant costs
associated with caring for these victims by authorizing courts to
require the accused to place funds in an account that can be accessed
by the sheltering organization to assist with providing this essential
service.

Under current law, once cruelty or animal fighting charges are filed,
it can be several months or even longer before the criminal case is
resolved - either by a plea bargain or by criminal trial. Depending
upon the specifics of the case and the jurisdiction, arraignment may
not occur for several days, several weeks, or in many cases much
longer. In New York City, for example, the typical wait for an
arraignment to occur is at least 6 to 8 weeks after the issuance of an
appearance ticket. This creates a clear and serious delay in the
ability to petition the court for security, thereby placing the
financial burden of caring for such animals squarely on the backs of
the impounding organization until arraignment occurs.

This legislation would authorize the security posting petition to be
filed upon the issuance of an appearance ticket or within a reasonable
time thereafter. It would not affect or confuse the current petition
process where an alleged abuser is brought into physical custody. The
proposal would also provide much-needed clarification for certain
jurisdictions (New York City in particular) that that the petition
shall be filed in the criminal court that will hear the pending
cruelty case.

Further, this legislation will benefit not just the impounding
organization and the seized animals but also the defendant, who will
be assured prompter access to the judicial forum to ensure retention
of his animals while criminal charges are resolved. Taken together,
these measures would greatly improve the process for animal shelters
and the local governments they serve to responsibly meet the costs
associated with caring for the victims of animal cruelty.

Unable to shoulder the costs associated with caring for these animals
alone, many shelters are forced to limit the assistance they can
offer. This creates an obstacle to effective enforcement of cruelty
and anti-fighting laws, which are serious misdemeanor and felony-level
crimes in New York State. If there is no place for the seized animals
to go, law enforcement often has little choice but to weigh against
seizing them in the first place, an outcome that must be avoided
wherever possible.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately.

summary: Provides for the filing and determination of a petition for the posting of security by persons against whom criminal charges are pending as the result of a crime against the animal.
